sessions.title: Hear a source enter the argument
sessions.summary: Recognize an attribution or citation as a change in the source field of a discussion.

source.translation: The Mishnah relies on a verse, as it is written.
source.note: A short signal can tell a reader that the discussion is grounding itself in another source.

questions.prompt: What should you expect after this attribution signal?
choices: A source will be brought to ground or explain the discussion.
A new unrelated story will begin.
The argument is finished.
questions.explanation: Attribution and citation signals tell the reader that evidence is entering.

questions.prompt: Why does recognizing an attribution phrase matter before full translation?
choices: It predicts the line’s argumentative job and the kind of material that follows.
It eliminates the need to read context.
It supplies a personal ruling.
questions.explanation: Signals help a learner map an argument before every word is secure.

sessions.title: Address, praise, and petition
sessions.summary: Distinguish what a prayer line does before asking what it means to the learner.

source.hebrew: ברוך אתה ה׳ אלהינו ואלהי אבותינו
source.translation: Blessed are You, the Lord our God and God of our ancestors.
source.note: Prayer has structure: address, praise, petition, thanks, and response each make different claims on attention.

questions.prompt: What is this line doing before it makes a request?
choices: Addressing God in a language of praise and inherited relationship.
Presenting a Mishnah case.
Distinguishing two damages categories.
questions.explanation: A reader first identifies prayer’s function rather than forcing it into another genre.

questions.prompt: What reading question helps when prayer turns from praise to petition?
choices: What need is voiced, and how does the form of address shape that request?
Which legal ruling follows immediately?
Which word is longest?
questions.explanation: Function helps a learner read prayer as structured speech.

sessions.title: A verse has a later life
sessions.summary: Return to Torah with attention to how a later source receives, narrows, or extends it.

source.translation: You shall eat, be satisfied, and bless.
source.note: A Torah directive can become the beginning of a source chain rather than the end of inquiry.

questions.prompt: What does a later source add to a Torah directive?
choices: A new framing, question, or specification that must be read in relation to the earlier source.
Proof that the Torah source no longer matters.
An excuse to skip the intervening argument.
questions.explanation: Reception adds context and reasoning; it does not erase the earlier verse.

questions.prompt: What should remain visible in a source chain?
choices: Original setting, later use, and the reasoning that connects them.
Only the final formulation.
Only a learner’s reaction.
questions.explanation: Canon literacy follows the movement between sources.

sessions.title: Audience changes the question
sessions.summary: Read a historical source by locating who is addressed before applying its language elsewhere.

source.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
source.note: The verse addresses a community in exile; that audience and setting matter for responsible reading.

questions.prompt: Which fact changes how you first read this command?
choices: It addresses a displaced community living in a particular city and historical situation.
It has no audience or setting.
It is a Gemara proof text.
questions.explanation: Historical context helps a reader avoid turning a source into a slogan.

questions.prompt: Why identify a source’s community and institution?
choices: They can explain which practical and intellectual questions the source is answering.
They make the text less Jewish.
They replace close reading of the words.
questions.explanation: Context and close reading belong together.

sessions.title: Let one word become a question
sessions.summary: Practice holding a compact word still long enough to see the question it creates.

source.note: A Gemara can turn on a single word when its meaning changes the source’s timing or category.

questions.prompt: What should a reader do before choosing a translation?
choices: Ask which possible meaning changes the case and why the Gemara pauses here.
Treat the word as decorative.
Look for a final ruling without reading the question.
questions.explanation: A word-question is an argument move, not a vocabulary flashcard.

questions.prompt: How does a close word-question transfer to another sugya?
choices: Look for the precise term whose meaning the discussion cannot take for granted.
Assume every short question is identical.
Translate only after deciding the conclusion.
questions.explanation: The habit transfers: identify the word under pressure and its role in the case.

sessions.title: A measurement has a purpose
sessions.summary: Read object, limit, response, and reason as one structured source move.

source.hebrew: מבוי שהוא גבוה למעלה מעשרים אמה ימעט
source.translation: An alleyway whose entrance is higher than twenty cubits must be lowered.
source.note: A number is not a lesson by itself; it belongs to an object, a condition, and a reason.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest first map of this line?
choices: Name the object, measured condition, response, then ask what purpose the limit serves.
Memorize twenty without the case.
Treat the number as a metaphor before reading further.
questions.explanation: Measure reading joins concrete description to reasoning.

questions.prompt: What should you compare when another tractate also uses twenty cubits?
choices: The structure, outcome, and reason—not merely the repeated number.
Only which tractate is longer.
Nothing; parallel sources cannot teach each other.
questions.explanation: Parallel cases sharpen purpose and distinction.

sessions.title: From validity to purpose
sessions.summary: Trace a physical ruling toward the source-based purpose that makes it intelligible.

source.hebrew: סוכה שהיא גבוהה למעלה מעשרים אמה פסולה
source.translation: A sukkah higher than twenty cubits is invalid.
source.note: The opening case leads to questions about why a physical condition matters.

questions.prompt: What question moves this source beyond memorizing a measurement?
choices: What reason or source-based purpose makes the condition relevant to validity?
Which modern practice it settles by itself.
Whether the number is easy to remember.
questions.explanation: A validity ruling invites the reader to seek its function and textual grounding.

questions.prompt: What role can a Torah verse play in explaining a physical requirement?
choices: It can supply a purpose or framing that makes the form intelligible.
It only decorates the discussion.
It makes every detail identical.
questions.explanation: A cited source must be read for the work it does in the argument.

sessions.title: Claims are not yet proof
sessions.summary: Keep parties, assertions, procedure, and evidence distinct in a dispute.

source.translation: Two people are holding a garment.
source.note: The Mishnah begins with a shared object and competing claims; the reader must not settle the dispute before mapping it.

questions.prompt: What should remain distinct in the first map?
choices: The object, each claimant’s assertion, and the later procedure or evidence.
A claim and proof, because they are the same.
The people, because only the garment matters.
questions.explanation: Dispute reading preserves the difference between asserting and establishing.

questions.prompt: What transfers from mapping a dispute to mapping another legal case?
choices: Keep people and their relations visible before applying a category.
Ignore the people and read only conclusions.
Assume one person’s position proves the result.
questions.explanation: Case-mapping is a portable legal reading habit.

sessions.title: Difference and shared principle
sessions.summary: Read categories by naming both the distinction and what still joins the cases.

source.translation: There are four primary categories of damage.
source.note: A counted opening establishes a field of categories before the discussion tests their differences and shared responsibility.

questions.prompt: Why name several primary categories before discussing a shared rule?
choices: To preserve meaningful differences before identifying a principle that joins them.
To prove all cases are identical.
To avoid reasoning about responsibility.
questions.explanation: Classification requires both distinction and connection.

questions.prompt: What similar move appears when a broad rule has an exception?
choices: Read the general category and the limiting distinction together.
Erase the rule because an exception exists.
Treat the exception as unrelated vocabulary.
questions.explanation: A limit can clarify rather than erase a category.

sessions.title: Procedure, concern, and proof
sessions.summary: Map a ritual procedure as an argument about preparation, risk, and textual grounding.

source.hebrew: שבעת ימים קודם יום הכפורים מפרישין כהן גדול מביתו
source.translation: Seven days before Yom Kippur, they separate the High Priest from his home.
source.note: Study the source’s procedure and reasoning; this is not present-day ritual guidance.

questions.prompt: What should you map after identifying the procedure?
choices: The role, safeguard, concern, limiting objection, and later proof text.
A personal ritual plan.
Only the number of days.
questions.explanation: Yoma trains a reader to see procedure as a structured argument.

questions.prompt: What does the Gemara’s source question ask for?
choices: The scriptural ground and phrase-by-phrase reasoning for the procedure.
A new unrelated narrative.
A reason to ignore the Mishnah.
questions.explanation: Proof-text reading joins a procedure to its textual argument.

sessions.title: Terms guide interpretations
sessions.summary: Define a conceptual term before treating disagreement as merely personal preference.

source.translation: Know today and bring it back to your heart.
source.note: The line invites questions about knowledge, inwardness, and the movement from awareness to commitment.

questions.prompt: Why clarify a term such as knowledge before comparing interpretations?
choices: Different definitions create different claims and questions about the same source.
Definitions make sources unnecessary.
A term can only have one possible use.
questions.explanation: Careful comparison begins by clarifying concepts.

questions.prompt: What should a reader ask when two sources use a shared word differently?
choices: What each source means by it and what evidence supports that reading.
Which source uses it more often.
Whether context can be ignored.
questions.explanation: Shared vocabulary can conceal real differences.

sessions.title: Compare without caricature
sessions.summary: Give two readings their strongest form before naming a genuine divergence.

source.note: Use a simple map to make disagreement more precise rather than louder.

questions.prompt: What makes a comparison responsible?
choices: State the shared question and the exact claim or reason where the readings diverge.
Treat both readings as interchangeable.
Choose the more familiar reader without evidence.
questions.explanation: Comparison preserves both connection and difference.

questions.prompt: What should a learner avoid in a conceptual disagreement?
choices: Reducing each view to a slogan before reading its sources and terms.
Naming context.
Asking what question both views share.
questions.explanation: Strong comparison resists caricature.

sessions.title: A source can call for a practice
sessions.summary: Connect a character source to a modest practice while keeping ethical reflection distinct from legal ruling.

source.translation: Do not separate from the community.
source.note: An ethical maxim can invite reflection and practice; it should not be used as an automatic answer to every case.

questions.prompt: What is a responsible first application?
choices: Name the value and try a modest practice while preserving the source’s limits and context.
Use the line to judge every individual situation immediately.
Treat it as a technical measurement.
questions.explanation: Ethical reading can guide practice without pretending to resolve every case.

questions.prompt: What joins close reading to character work?
choices: A source claim, its reason, and a small practice that can be revisited.
A final answer that needs no reflection.
Avoiding any concrete action.
questions.explanation: Mussar makes attention actionable in modest ways.

sessions.title: Texts live in institutions
sessions.summary: See community, language, place, and institutions as part of the questions a source can ask.

source.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
source.note: A source addressed to a community can become more legible when its historical setting is kept visible.

questions.prompt: What historical question belongs beside close reading?
choices: Which community, conditions, and institutions make this address urgent?
Which modern conclusion is automatic?
Which genre has no context?
questions.explanation: Institutions and settings shape the questions communities face.

questions.prompt: Why can language and location matter for later Jewish texts?
choices: They help explain audiences, available resources, and the shape of a discussion.
They erase the text’s ideas.
They make all sources identical.
questions.explanation: History is evidence for reading, not background decoration.

sessions.title: Compare traditions as sources
sessions.summary: Use the same disciplined comparison with Jewish and wider intellectual canons.

source.citation: Judaism and the wider world study protocol
source.note: A responsible comparison begins with sources and preserves real differences; it is not a claim that traditions collapse into one language.

questions.prompt: What is the first discipline of a comparison?
choices: Name a shared question while preserving each source’s setting and difference.
Assume influence from a vague resemblance.
Use only stereotypes.
questions.explanation: Comparison is careful reading across contexts.

questions.prompt: What should a learner ask about intellectual exchange?
choices: How language, institutions, and translation shaped what could be received and read.
Which culture has no internal diversity.
Whether texts appear without communities.
questions.explanation: Ideas travel through real historical settings.

sessions.title: Trace one question across forms
sessions.summary: Follow a question from Torah through Gemara, prayer, practice, and reflection without making the sources identical.

source.note: The same words can be Torah address, Mishnah practice, Gemara problem, and liturgical recitation; each setting adds a question.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest way to connect these settings?
choices: Name what each source form contributes while preserving its distinct voice and context.
Treat the latest use as the only meaning.
Assume every setting asks the same question.
questions.explanation: Integration builds relation without erasing difference.

questions.prompt: What does a source chain teach a learner to do?
choices: Trace reception, reasoning, and practice through multiple stages of the canon.
Stop at the first familiar line.
Replace context with a slogan.
questions.explanation: A canon is a conversation across forms and times.

sessions.title: Meet an unfamiliar sugya
sessions.summary: Use your repertoire on a page you have not rehearsed line by line.

source.note: These labels help a learner create a first map; they do not replace attention to the actual source.

questions.prompt: What is the responsible first pass through an unfamiliar sugya?
choices: Locate case and source signals, label likely moves, then use translation to verify.
Guess a ruling before reading the source.
Wait until every word is known before mapping anything.
questions.explanation: Independent reading uses supports deliberately and names uncertainty honestly.

questions.prompt: What should a learner do with one unresolved line?
choices: State the uncertainty, preserve the map, and choose a targeted next resource or question.
Pretend it is understood.
Discard the entire source.
questions.explanation: Responsible independence includes knowing what remains unclear.

sessions.title: Choose the next question responsibly
sessions.summary: Use Seder’s tools to decide whether the next move is retrieval, a new source, a repair, or further guidance.

source.note: Independent study is not isolation. A strong learner knows when to retrieve, clarify, compare, and seek appropriate help.

questions.prompt: What should determine a learner’s next move after an unfamiliar source?
choices: The evidence: whether a move is secure, uncertain, due for retrieval, or needs a better question or guidance.
Only which lesson is shortest.
A claim of mastery without evidence.
questions.explanation: Mastery learning chooses the next source task from demonstrated need.

questions.prompt: When a source raises practical or personal stakes, what does responsible independence include?
choices: Recognizing the limit of the study exercise and seeking appropriate qualified guidance or community.
Treating an app lesson as a personal ruling.
Avoiding all questions.
questions.explanation: Independence includes knowing when learning requires other people and forms of authority.
